definition: Negation: 'not' - true exactly when p is false
Conjunction: 'and' - true exactly when both p and q are true
Disjunction: 'or' (inclusive) - true when p or q or both are true
Implication: 'if ... then ...' - false only when p is true and q is false
Biconditional: 'if and only if' - true exactly when p and q have the same truth value
Implication (alternative notation): 'if ... then ...', same connective as U+2192
Equivalence: 'is equivalent to' - p and q have the same truth value in every case
Falsum: the constant false proposition, always false; also marks a contradiction
Verum: the constant true proposition, always true
Proves: p can be derived (proved) from the premises by the rules of the system
Entails: p is true in every interpretation in which all the premises are true
Therefore: marks the conclusion of an argument
Because: marks a reason or premise for a claim
Exclusive or (circled-plus form): true exactly when exactly one of p, q is true
Exclusive or: true exactly when exactly one of p, q is true
Sheffer stroke (NAND): 'not (p and q)' - true except when both p and q are true
Does not prove: p cannot be derived from the premises
Does not entail: p is not a semantic consequence of the premises
